\chapter{The Breath That Is a Letter}
\label{ch:bn-breath-is-a-letter}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write eight Bengali consonants as cells of one grid — lips, teeth, roof and throat, each with the voice and the breath switched on or off — and read \bn{আবার} and \bn{ভালো} with them.}

The eighth consonant closes a grid rather than lengthening a list: the chapter's whole set written back from the four places of articulation, with the two words it made readable.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bô]{\bn{ব} — the consonant ba}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-ba}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\bn{কেমন}} aloud before adding a new shape, and say which way its vowel sign faces.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ব}
\end{quote}

\textbf{bô} — the \emph{b} of English \emph{bin}, with the lips shut and no puff of air after.

This shape carries the load of the track's whole sound-fingerprint. Sanskrit had a separate \emph{v}, and Bengali does not: the sound collapsed into \textbf{b}, and the letter that used to write \emph{v} is now read as this one. That is why Sanskrit \emph{dhanyavāda} is spoken \emph{dhônyobad} in the first chapter, and why a Sanskrit word with a \emph{v} in it will keep turning up in Bengali with a \emph{b}.

So when a word looks like a Sanskrit word you know but has a \emph{b} where you expect a \emph{v}, you have not found a different word. You have found the same one, wearing this letter.

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ব}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{বা}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ব}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{বা}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{কেমন}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit sound does \textbf{\bn{ব}} now do the work of, besides \emph{b}? (\emph{\textbf{v}}.) So if a Sanskrit word you know has a \emph{v} where Bengali has a \emph{b}, is it a different word? (\textbf{No} — the same one.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ābār]{\bn{আবার} — again, read}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-abar-read}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{ব}}, and say which Sanskrit sound it took over.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আ}} + \textbf{\bn{ব}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} + \textbf{\bn{র}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{আবার}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{আ}} — standing alone at the front of the word, as it always must
  \item \textbf{\bn{ব}} with \textbf{\bn{া}} — \emph{bā}
  \item \textbf{\bn{র}} — \emph{rô}, worn down to almost nothing at the end
\end{itemize}

\textbf{ābār} — \emph{again}, the word that opens the goodbye from the farewells chapter.

Two things are worth noticing about the shape of the word rather than its meaning.

First, the \textbf{\bn{আ}} at the front. A vowel at the start of a word has no consonant to hang a sign on, so it uses its own full independent letter. A vowel anywhere else is a sign. Same sound, two forms, and which one you write is decided entirely by whether there is a consonant to lean on.

Second, look at the two \textbf{\bn{া}} shapes here — no, look again: there is only one. The first \textbf{\bn{আ}} contains a vertical stroke that resembles the mātrā, and it is not one. That resemblance is not an accident of the font. The independent letter and the sign are historically the same mark, which is exactly why they look related and exactly why they are easy to confuse.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{আবার}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{আবার} \bn{আমার}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{আবার}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \textbf{\bn{আবার}} open with the full letter \textbf{\bn{আ}} and not the sign \textbf{\bn{া}}? (There is \textbf{no consonant to lean on} at the start of a word.) And what does the word mean? (\emph{\textbf{Again}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhô]{\bn{ভ} — the consonant bha, the breathy twin}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-bha}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\bn{আবার}}, and write \textbf{\bn{ব}} once from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ভ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{bhô} — \textbf{\bn{ব}} with a puff of breath released through it. Not \emph{b} then \emph{h} as two sounds, but one closure opened onto a gust.

The letter for the unaspirated \textbf{\bn{ক}} made this point about \emph{k} in the last script chapter, and here it is again on the other side of the mouth: \textbf{the puff is a letter, not a manner of speaking.} Hold a palm in front of your mouth. Say English \emph{bin}: no air. Now push a breath out through the release. That is this shape.

English has both sounds and treats neither as meaningful — the \emph{b} of \emph{bin} and an emphatic, breathy \emph{b} are the same word said twice. Bengali has two letters, two spellings, and two words.

Look at the shape beside the one it is built from. \textbf{\bn{ব}} and \textbf{\bn{ভ}} share their left-hand body; \textbf{\bn{ভ}} adds a stroke on the right. The script is drawing the relationship the mouth makes, which is a habit worth expecting: aspirated letters often look like their plain partners with something extra.

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভ}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{ভা}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ভ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ব} \bn{ভ}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{আবার}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the puff of breath in \textbf{\bn{ভ}} a separate sound or part of the letter? (\textbf{Part of the letter}.) Does English treat the difference as meaningful? (\textbf{No}.) Does Bengali? (\textbf{Yes} — two letters, two words.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhālo]{\bn{ভালো} — good, read}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-bhalo-read}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{ব}} and \textbf{\bn{ভ}} one after the other, and say what separates them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভ}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} + \textbf{\bn{ল}} + \textbf{\bn{ো}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{ভালো}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{ভ}} with \textbf{\bn{া}} — \emph{bhā}, breath and all
  \item \textbf{\bn{ল}} with \textbf{\bn{ো}} around it — \emph{lo}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{bhālo} — \emph{good, well}. It is the answer to \emph{how are you}; it is the first half of the phrase for liking something; it is the first half of the verb for loving someone. No word in this track turns up in more sentences.

Now put it next to the word from two lessons ago, and beside the possessive from the introductions chapter:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আবার}} — \emph{ābār}, again \textbf{\bn{আমার}} — \emph{āmār}, my
\end{quote}

Identical except for the middle letter. A learner who can build one has built the other, and a learner who cannot yet tell \textbf{\bn{ব}} from \textbf{\bn{ম}} at a glance has now been handed the exercise that fixes it. \textbf{\bn{ভালো}} sets the same trap with its own first letter, and a later chapter will spring it on a colour word built to the same pattern.

That near-miss is worth taking seriously rather than enjoying. Bengali is full of pairs like this, and the reader who slows down for the first letter is the reader who stops guessing words from their silhouette.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{ভালো}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{আবার} \bn{আমার}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ভালো}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the only difference on the page between \textbf{\bn{আবার}} and \textbf{\bn{আমার}}? (\textbf{The middle letter}.) And which piece of \textbf{\bn{ভালো}} would you have to change to get a different word? (\textbf{The first letter} — every one of these near-pairs turns on a single shape.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khô]{\bn{খ} — the consonant kha, the breathy k}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-kha}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\bn{ভালো}}, then write \textbf{\bn{ক}} from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{খ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{khô} — \textbf{\bn{ক}} with the breath let out through it. The \emph{k} of English \emph{kit}, in fact, which is the breathy one; \textbf{\bn{ক}} was the \emph{k} of \emph{skip}.

That makes three pairs met so far, and the third is where a pattern earns the name:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{ক}} plain, \textbf{\bn{খ}} breathy
  \item \textbf{\bn{ব}} plain, \textbf{\bn{ভ}} breathy
\end{itemize}

Bengali sorts its consonants into families this way all the way down, and it does it in a fixed order that every Indian script shares — which is why a Bengali dictionary, a Devanagari dictionary and a Tamil dictionary all run their letters in the same sequence, though the shapes have nothing in common.

Knowing that a plain letter has a breathy partner turns a list of forty shapes into twenty pairs, and pairs are what a hand can hold.

With the u-sign underneath:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{খ}} + \textbf{\bn{ু}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{খু}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{খ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ক} \bn{খ}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{ভালো}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\bn{ক}} and \textbf{\bn{খ}} is the \emph{k} of \emph{kit}? (\textbf{\bn{খ}} — the breathy one.) And what does knowing about pairs do to a list of forty shapes? (Turns it into \textbf{twenty pairs}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pô]{\bn{প} — the consonant pa}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-pa}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{খ}} from memory, and say what separates it from \textbf{\bn{ক}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{প}
\end{quote}

\textbf{pô} — the \emph{p} of English \emph{spin}, lips shut, no puff of air after the release.

The place is the lips, which is where \textbf{\bn{ব}} was made too. So the two of them fill two cells of one square:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{প}} — lips, voice off
  \item \textbf{\bn{ব}} — lips, voice on
\end{itemize}

The English \emph{p} of \emph{pin} is the breathy one and belongs to a different letter, the same trap \textbf{\bn{ক}} and \textbf{\bn{খ}} laid a lesson ago. Palm in front of the mouth: \emph{spin} gives no air, and that is this letter.

With the lips named, the map is complete. Every consonant this book has taught is made at one of four places — \textbf{lips, teeth, roof, throat} — and every one of them is one of four cells at that place. A reader who has that grid is not memorising forty unrelated shapes. They are filling in a table.

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{প}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{পা}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{প}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{প} \bn{ব}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{ভালো}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is \textbf{\bn{প}} made? (\textbf{At the lips}.) Which other letter is made there? (\textbf{\bn{ব}}.) And what separates them? (\textbf{The voice}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dô]{\bn{দ} — the consonant da}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-da}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{খ}} and \textbf{\bn{প}}, then write \textbf{\bn{ত}} and say where the tongue goes for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{দ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{dô} — the same tongue position as \textbf{\bn{ত}}, on the \textbf{back of the top front teeth}, with the voice switched on.

So the warning that came with \textbf{\bn{ত}} applies here without a word changed. English makes its \emph{d} on the ridge behind the teeth; Bengali has a separate letter for that position, and it is a different letter spelling different words. Slide the tongue forward onto enamel.

The pair to hold is not \emph{t} and \emph{d} as English thinks of them. It is:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{ত}} dental, voice off
  \item \textbf{\bn{দ}} dental, voice on
\end{itemize}

Two settings on one place of articulation. Bengali's consonant grid is built out of exactly these two switches — where the tongue is, and whether the voice is on — plus the breath from the last lesson. Three switches, and most of the inventory falls out of them.

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দ}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{দা}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{দ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ত} \bn{দ}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{ভালো} \bn{আবার}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the same about \textbf{\bn{ত}} and \textbf{\bn{দ}}? (\textbf{Where the tongue goes} — the teeth.) What is different? (\textbf{The voice}.) And is an English \emph{d} the same letter? (\textbf{No} — it is made further back.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhô]{\bn{ধ} — the consonant dha}

\label{lesson:BN-W03-dha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{দ}} from memory, and say where the tongue touches for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ধ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{dhô} — \textbf{\bn{দ}} with the breath let out through it. Voice on, tongue on the teeth, and air after the release.

Set the four dental letters side by side and the grid the last two lessons have been building is visible in one line:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{ত}} — voice off, no breath
  \item \textbf{\bn{দ}} — voice on, no breath
  \item \textbf{\bn{ধ}} — voice on, with breath
\end{itemize}

The fourth cell, voice off and with breath, is a letter this book has not needed yet. It exists, it sits between the first two in every dictionary, and it will arrive when a word calls for it.

\textbf{That square is the unit.} Every place of articulation in the script — teeth, ridge, palate, throat — gets the same four cells in the same order, and the order is over two thousand years old: the Sanskrit grammarians sorted the sounds by where they were made and wrote the list down, and every script descended from that tradition still lists them that way.

With the u-sign:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ধ}} + \textbf{\bn{ু}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{ধু}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \bn{ধ}
  \item \bn{ত} \bn{দ} \bn{ধ}
  \item \bn{দা} \bn{ধা}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things separate \textbf{\bn{ধ}} from \textbf{\bn{ত}}? (\textbf{Voice} and \textbf{breath}.) How many cells does one place of articulation get? (\textbf{Four}.) And who fixed that order? (The \textbf{Sanskrit grammarians}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chô]{\bn{চ} — the consonant cha}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-cha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{দ}} and \textbf{\bn{ধ}}, and say which of the two lets the breath out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{চ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{chô} — the \emph{ch} of English \emph{cheap}, with no puff of air after it.

The tongue is somewhere new. Not on the teeth, where \textbf{\bn{ত}} and \textbf{\bn{দ}} are made, and not at the back, where \textbf{\bn{ক}} is: the body of the tongue comes up flat against the \textbf{hard roof of the mouth}, a little behind the ridge. English spells that place with two letters, \emph{ch}, because its alphabet has no single sign for it. Bengali has one letter, and — following the square this chapter has been filling — a breathy partner and two voiced cells to go with it.

That is the fourth place of articulation this book has named: teeth, roof, throat, and lips. The list is not long. \textbf{Everything the script writes is one of those places with the voice and breath switches set.}

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চ}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{চা}}
\end{quote}

That is already a word, and it gets its own lesson next.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{চ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{চা}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{কেমন} \bn{ভালো}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where in the mouth is \textbf{\bn{চ}} made? (Against the \textbf{roof}, behind the ridge.) How many letters does English need for that sound? (\textbf{Two}.) And Bengali? (\textbf{One}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jô]{\bn{জ} — the consonant ja, and the eight this chapter added}

\label{lesson:BN-W04-ja}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{চ}}, and say where on the roof of the mouth it is made.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{জ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{jô} — the \emph{j} of English \emph{jam}. Same place as \textbf{\bn{চ}}, the flat of the tongue on the roof of the mouth, with the voice on.

Another two cells of another square, and by now the move should be predictable: meet a consonant, ask where it is made and whether the voice is running, and the letter has a family rather than being a shape on its own.

This letter carries a root worth knowing. Sanskrit \emph{jñā}, \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} is spelled with it, and the verbs chapter followed that root out to English \textbf{know} and to the \emph{k} that English still writes and no longer says. The Bengali verb for knowing facts opens on this shape.

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জ}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{জা}}
\end{quote}

That is the chapter's eighth and last consonant, and it closes a grid rather than lengthening a list. Every one of the eight was met as a cell — a place in the mouth, with the voice and the breath switched on or off. Say them back by place rather than by shape:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{at the lips}: \textbf{\bn{প}} voice off, \textbf{\bn{ব}} voice on, \textbf{\bn{ভ}} voice on with breath
  \item \textbf{on the teeth}: \textbf{\bn{দ}} voice on, \textbf{\bn{ধ}} voice on with breath
  \item \textbf{on the roof}: \textbf{\bn{চ}} voice off, \textbf{\bn{জ}} voice on
  \item \textbf{at the throat}: \textbf{\bn{খ}}, voice off and breathy — \textbf{\bn{ক}}'s partner from the first script chapter
\end{itemize}

The cells nobody has filled are letters this book has not needed yet, not gaps in the script. A reader who can recite that list by place is filling in a grid; a reader holding eight shapes is memorising eight shapes. That difference is the whole reason the chapter kept asking \emph{where} and \emph{with what breath} instead of \emph{what does this look like}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{জ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{চ} \bn{জ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ব} \bn{ভ} \bn{খ} \bn{প} \bn{দ} \bn{ধ} \bn{চ} \bn{জ}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \bn{আবার} \bn{ভালো}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \textbf{\bn{জ}} from \textbf{\bn{চ}}? (\textbf{The voice}.) How many consonants did this chapter add? (\textbf{Eight}.) And what question does the grid ask of a new letter — what it looks like, or where it is made? (\textbf{Where it is made}, and with what breath.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
